title: Feelings
hookLine: pleasant, painful, neither; worldly and unworldly (MN 10)

lines: BEFORE YOU KNOW WHAT IT IS.
cards: Buddhist teachers point to a moment that comes very fast: before a thing is even named, it already feels good, bad, or neither.
A song starts, and before its name comes to mind, something may already have leaned in or pulled back. A smell drifts out of a kitchen: yes, or no.
A text lights up your phone, and there's a little flicker of good or bad before you've read a word. That flicker is easy to miss, and in the Buddha's teaching it steers what comes next.
The Satipatthana Sutta makes it the second foundation.

teach.b: Vedana is usually translated feeling, but it doesn't mean emotions like joy or anger.
It means the feeling tone of any experience: pleasant, painful, or neither pleasant nor painful. In Buddhist teaching, every sight, sound, smell, taste, touch and thought comes with one of the three.
The instruction is simple. Feeling a pleasant feeling, the practitioner knows, I feel a pleasant feeling. Feeling a painful one, they know it.
Feeling one that's neither, they know that too.
Then a second layer: each feeling can be worldly or unworldly. Worldly feelings are tied to ordinary things, like the pleasure of good food or the pain of an insult.
Unworldly ones come from practice itself: the quiet joy of a calm mind, or the ache of wanting to be free. Then the chorus: inside, outside, arising and passing away. Why a whole foundation?

teach.h: FEELING IS THE HINGE TO CRAVING.
teach.b: Because in Buddhist teaching, feeling is the hinge. In the chain the Buddha called dependent origination, feeling gives rise to craving.

Pleasant feeling tends to spark wanting more. Painful feeling tends to spark pushing away. Neutral feeling, the texts say, has ignorance lying behind it: it slips past unnoticed, and attention drifts off.
Catch the feeling while it's still just a feeling, before it becomes a want or a push, and you've found a gap. In that gap, you get a choice.

how: Many insight meditation teachers have students note the feeling tone of experiences as pleasant, unpleasant or neutral, since Buddhist teaching places vedana just before craving in the chain of dependent origination.

o: a gut hunch about whether someone is honest
a strong emotion like joy, anger, fear or grief
the tone of an experience: pleasant, painful, neither

games.q: match each kind of feeling to an example.
p: the quiet joy of a calm mind
a plain moment, not good or bad

s: vedana means emotions like love and anger
it means feeling tone: pleasant, painful, or neither.
in dependent origination, feeling gives rise to craving
that's why catching the feeling opens a gap.
the sutta divides feelings into worldly and unworldly too
tied to ordinary things, or arising from practice itself.

games.q: you taste something delicious and immediately reach for more. where in that moment does the sutta suggest looking?
o: at the pleasant feeling itself, before the reach.
games.why: knowing the pleasant feeling as a feeling, before craving takes over, is the whole second foundation.

practice: Let your attention move around the body and the room, and each time something catches you, a sound, an ache, the warmth of your hands, a thought, give it one quiet label: pleasant, painful, or neither.
Don't explain it or change it; just label it and let it go. You may notice how many things are simply neither, and that's normal.

wordCard.voice: Vedana. The feeling tone of every experience: pleasant, painful, or neither. The hinge between what happens and what we want.

orig.note: Pali vedanā: feeling tone, pleasant, painful or neither.

carryVoice: Your line: pleasant, painful, neither. Three tones, running under everything you meet. See you tomorrow.

sources.ref: Majjhima Nikāya 10 (Satipaṭṭhāna Sutta), contemplation of feelings
